prompt: Which of these explains why a page loads slowly, rather than describing that it does?
optionA: The page takes a long time to appear
optionB: The page requests forty separate images, each needing its own round trip
optionC: The page has poor loading performance
optionD: A page is a document fetched over a network
correctAnswerText: The page requests forty separate images, each needing its own round trip
explanation: An explanation names something that produces the effect. Restating the slowness in other words is circular, and defining what a page is answers a different question.

prompt: Which of these explains why a total came out wrong, rather than describing that it did?
optionA: The total is not the correct value
optionB: The program has a bug in its arithmetic
optionC: A total is the sum of a set of values
optionD: The running total was reset inside the loop, so only the last value survived
correctAnswerText: The running total was reset inside the loop, so only the last value survived
explanation: Only one option names a mechanism that would produce the wrong total. "Has a bug" restates the symptom in technical-sounding words without saying anything about it.

prompt: Which of these explains why a file is still on disk after a program closes?
optionA: Saving writes the data to storage, which keeps its contents without power
optionB: Files are persistent
optionC: The file was not deleted
optionD: A file is a named collection of data
correctAnswerText: Saving writes the data to storage, which keeps its contents without power
explanation: Saving writes the data to storage, which keeps its contents without power — that names why the file is still there. "Files are persistent" is the observation dressed as a reason, and the others are a definition and a statement of what did not occur.

prompt: What makes a statement an explanation rather than a description?
optionA: It uses technical vocabulary
optionB: It is longer than a description
optionC: It says why something happens, not only what happens
optionD: It is written for an expert reader
correctAnswerText: It says why something happens, not only what happens
explanation: Explanations answer why. Vocabulary, length and audience are all properties an explanation may have without being one.

prompt: Someone says a program is slow "because it has performance problems". Why is that not an explanation?
optionA: It is too short to be an explanation
optionB: It restates the observation in different words, so nothing new is offered as a cause
optionC: It uses vocabulary the reader may not know
optionD: It is an explanation, though not a detailed one
correctAnswerText: It restates the observation in different words, so nothing new is offered as a cause
explanation: A cause has to be something other than the effect, and this is the effect renamed. Length and vocabulary are beside the point — a one-word cause would still be an explanation.

prompt: Working memory is described as a desk and storage as a filing cabinet. What does taking a folder out of the cabinet and putting it on the desk correspond to?
optionA: Saving a file from working memory to storage
optionB: Deleting a file
optionC: Switching the machine off
optionD: Loading a file from storage into working memory
correctAnswerText: Loading a file from storage into working memory
explanation: The direction matters: the cabinet is the long-term place and the desk is where work happens, so moving from cabinet to desk is loading. Reversing the direction gives saving.

prompt: A queue is described as a line of people waiting. What does the front of the line correspond to?
optionA: The item that will be dealt with next
optionB: The item added most recently
optionC: The item that has already been dealt with
optionD: The total number of items waiting
correctAnswerText: The item that will be dealt with next
explanation: People join a line at the back and are served from the front, so the front is what comes next. The most recent arrival is at the other end.

prompt: A network is described as a postal system. What does an address correspond to?
optionA: The contents of the message
optionB: The speed of delivery
optionC: The information that decides where the data is delivered
optionD: The person who wrote the message
correctAnswerText: The information that decides where the data is delivered
explanation: An address in both systems is what routing acts on. Contents and sender are carried along and play no part in deciding the destination.

prompt: A cache is described as a notepad on which you jot down answers you have looked up. What does the notepad becoming out of date correspond to?
optionA: The cache running out of space
optionB: A stored copy no longer matching what the source now says
optionC: The cache being cleared deliberately
optionD: The original source becoming unavailable
correctAnswerText: A stored copy no longer matching what the source now says
explanation: The mapping is between a jotted answer and a stored copy, and the failure mode is the same in both: the source changed and the note did not. Running out of space is a different situation with a different remedy.

prompt: An explanation for someone who has never programmed says: "The function is called recursively until the base case is reached." Which term would stop that reader?
optionA: called
optionB: until
optionC: reached
optionD: recursively
correctAnswerText: recursively
explanation: The three ordinary words carry their everyday meanings. Only one term has a technical sense the reader could not guess, and the sentence depends on it.

prompt: An explanation for a first-year student says: "The value is stored in a variable, then serialised before it is sent." Which term would stop that reader?
optionA: serialised
optionB: stored
optionC: variable
optionD: sent
correctAnswerText: serialised
explanation: A first-year has met variables and storing. Only one word here belongs to a later topic, and the reader has no way to guess it from context.

prompt: Is a long word necessarily jargon?
optionA: Yes; long words should be replaced
optionB: No; jargon is any word with more than three syllables
optionC: No; jargon is a term with a technical meaning the reader does not have, whatever its length
optionD: Yes, unless the reader is an expert
correctAnswerText: No; jargon is a term with a technical meaning the reader does not have, whatever its length
explanation: What makes a term jargon is the reader's unfamiliarity with its technical sense. Plenty of jargon is short — "heap", "thread", "commit" — and plenty of long words are ordinary.

prompt: An explanation defines "idempotent" in its first sentence and uses it in its fourth. Is the term jargon for a reader who has never met it?
optionA: Yes; the term is technical whatever the explanation does
optionB: Not by the fourth sentence; the explanation supplied the meaning before relying on it
optionC: Yes; a reader cannot learn a term from one definition
optionD: No; the term is not technical at all
correctAnswerText: Not by the fourth sentence; the explanation supplied the meaning before relying on it
explanation: Jargon is a property of the reader's knowledge at the moment they meet the word, and an explanation can change that. Defining before using is exactly what makes a technical term usable.

prompt: Three parts of an explanation: (a) what a variable is, (b) what assignment does, (c) why a total must be set before a loop. In which order does nothing depend on something unsaid?
optionA: c, a, b
optionB: b, a, c
optionC: c, b, a
optionD: a, b, c
correctAnswerText: a, b, c
explanation: Assignment needs a variable to have been introduced, and the point about the total needs both. Beginning with the conclusion leaves the reader holding a claim they cannot yet follow.

prompt: An explanation runs: "The cache serves the old copy, which is why the page is stale. A cache stores copies of files." What is wrong with the order?
optionA: The term is used to explain the symptom before the term itself is introduced
optionB: The two sentences should be joined into one
optionC: The explanation is too short
optionD: Nothing; the reader will infer the meaning
correctAnswerText: The term is used to explain the symptom before the term itself is introduced
explanation: The first sentence depends on the second, so the reader meets a load-bearing term with no meaning attached. Whether they can guess it is not the point — the order makes them guess.

prompt: An explanation reads: "When you save a file, the application writes it to the disk directly, and the operating system records its name." Which step is untrue?
optionA: The operating system recording the name
optionB: The file being written when you save
optionC: The application writing to the disk directly
optionD: None; the explanation is accurate
correctAnswerText: The application writing to the disk directly
explanation: Applications ask the operating system rather than reaching hardware, so that step is wrong while the others are right. The explanation reads perfectly well, which is why fluency cannot be the cue.

prompt: An explanation reads: "A loop checks its condition, runs its body, and repeats — so a loop always runs its body at least once." Which step is untrue?
optionA: That a loop checks its condition
optionB: The conclusion that the body always runs at least once
optionC: That a loop runs its body
optionD: That a loop repeats
correctAnswerText: The conclusion that the body always runs at least once
explanation: The first three steps describe a test-first loop accurately, and the conclusion contradicts them: if the condition is false at entry the body never runs. The false part is the one that sounds like a summary.

prompt: The question was "why did my change not appear?". The explanation says: "Browsers store copies of files." What step is missing?
optionA: That browsers can be closed and reopened
optionB: How caching improves performance
optionC: What a browser is
optionD: That the stored copy is being used instead of fetching the changed file
correctAnswerText: That the stored copy is being used instead of fetching the changed file
explanation: The reader has been told a fact and not how it produces their symptom. The other options are true and answer questions nobody asked.

prompt: The question was "why is my total wrong?". The explanation says: "You reset the total inside the loop." What step is missing?
optionA: That resetting inside the loop discards everything accumulated so far, leaving only the last value
optionB: Where the loop should be placed in the file
optionC: What a total is
optionD: How to write a loop
correctAnswerText: That resetting inside the loop discards everything accumulated so far, leaving only the last value
explanation: The reader has been told what they did and not why it produces this result, so they cannot recognise the same mistake elsewhere. The missing step is the link between the cause and the symptom.

prompt: The question was "should I use a fetch or a submitting method here?". The explanation accurately describes what each method means. It contains no false statements. What is missing?
optionA: A definition of a method
optionB: A description of how the request travels
optionC: What goes wrong if the wrong one is chosen, which is what the decision turns on
optionD: Nothing; the explanation is accurate
correctAnswerText: What goes wrong if the wrong one is chosen, which is what the decision turns on
explanation: Accuracy and completeness are separate, and this explanation is accurate about definitions while silent about consequences. The reader asked which to choose and has been given no ground for choosing.

prompt: Working memory is described as a desk. Which conclusion would that analogy wrongly support?
optionA: That the desk holds what you are working on now
optionB: That things left on the desk are still there tomorrow morning
optionC: That a bigger desk lets you work on more at once
optionD: That putting something away frees space
correctAnswerText: That things left on the desk are still there tomorrow morning
explanation: A desk keeps its contents overnight and working memory does not, so the analogy misleads at exactly that point. The other three conclusions hold in both.

prompt: A network is described as a postal system. Which conclusion would that analogy wrongly support?
optionA: That messages need an address
optionB: That messages may take different routes
optionC: That messages can be delayed
optionD: That only one copy of a message exists, so sending it means giving it away
correctAnswerText: That only one copy of a message exists, so sending it means giving it away
explanation: Posting a letter removes it from the sender and sending data copies it, so the analogy breaks over whether the original remains. The other three carry across correctly.

prompt: A cache is described as a notepad of jotted answers. A student concludes that clearing the cache loses information permanently. The analogy is otherwise sound and widely used. Why does the conclusion not follow?
optionA: A jotted note may be the only copy, while a cached copy always has a source it can be fetched from again
optionB: Because clearing a cache is impossible
optionC: Because a notepad is not a good analogy for a cache
optionD: Because the cache is stored on the server
correctAnswerText: A jotted note may be the only copy, while a cached copy always has a source it can be fetched from again
explanation: Every analogy carries some conclusions and not others, and this one breaks precisely where the original still exists. The analogy is genuinely useful, which is what makes knowing its limit necessary rather than a reason to discard it.

prompt: A first-year asks why their page will not load. The answer explains the details of how names are resolved into addresses. Is the depth right?
optionA: Yes; more detail is always better
optionB: No; it is not deep enough
optionC: No; it is too deep for the question, which was about their page rather than about resolution
optionD: Yes; the reader will learn something useful
correctAnswerText: No; it is too deep for the question, which was about their page rather than about resolution
explanation: Depth is judged against what was asked, and an accurate answer to a different question does not become right by being informative. The reader leaves without knowing why their page fails.

prompt: An experienced developer asks why a particular request is being refused. The answer says "something went wrong with the request". Is the depth right?
optionA: Yes; short answers are clearer
optionB: No; it is too shallow for this reader and this question, which needed the specific reason
optionC: No; the answer is inaccurate
optionD: Yes; the reader can investigate further
correctAnswerText: No; it is too shallow for this reader and this question, which needed the specific reason
explanation: The answer is true and tells the reader nothing they did not already know. What the depth has to match is both the question and what the reader can already do with it.

prompt: A first-year asks "why does my loop never end?". The answer explains, accurately, how a processor executes instructions in a cycle. The answer is entirely correct. What is wrong with it?
optionA: It is inaccurate about the processor
optionB: It is too short for the question
optionC: Nothing; the explanation is correct
optionD: It answers a question about the program with an explanation about the machine, so the reader still cannot fix their loop
correctAnswerText: It answers a question about the program with an explanation about the machine, so the reader still cannot fix their loop
explanation: Correctness does not make an explanation an answer. The reader needs to know that nothing in their body changes the condition, and no amount of accurate detail about the processor supplies that.

prompt: Why does a program stop with a division by zero? Which account names a cause?
optionA: A count used as the divisor was zero, because the list it counted was empty
optionB: Because a division by zero occurred
optionC: Because the program has a fault
optionD: Because division is a risky operation
correctAnswerText: A count used as the divisor was zero, because the list it counted was empty
explanation: Only one account says something other than the effect. "A division by zero occurred" is the observation restated, which is circular however technical it sounds.

prompt: Why is a page showing yesterday's data? Which account names a cause?
optionA: Because the page is out of date
optionB: Because caching exists
optionC: The browser reused a stored copy rather than requesting the file again
optionD: Because pages sometimes show old content
correctAnswerText: The browser reused a stored copy rather than requesting the file again
explanation: A cause has to be something that happened. That caching exists is a fact about the world and not about this page, and the other two restate the symptom.

prompt: Why did a nightly job fail? One account says "because the disk was full". Another says "because a log file grew without limit and filled the disk". Both are true. Which is the more useful explanation, and why?
optionA: The first, because it is the immediate cause
optionB: The second, because it names something that can be changed; the first names a state that will recur
optionC: The first, because it is simpler
optionD: They are equally useful, since both are true
correctAnswerText: The second, because it names something that can be changed; the first names a state that will recur
explanation: Both are accurate and they sit at different distances from something actionable. Clearing the disk addresses the first and the job fails again next week; limiting the log addresses the second.

prompt: Which example best demonstrates that a loop can run zero times?
optionA: A loop counting from 1 to 10
optionB: A loop that never ends
optionC: A loop containing a conditional
optionD: A loop counting from 1 to 0, whose condition is false before the first pass
correctAnswerText: A loop counting from 1 to 0, whose condition is false before the first pass
explanation: The concept is a loop whose body never runs, and only one option shows it. The others are genuine examples of other things.

prompt: Which example best demonstrates that copying a variable does not link the two?
optionA: a is set to 5, b is set to a, a is then set to 10, and b is still 5
optionB: a is set to 5 and b is set to 5
optionC: a is set to 5 and printed twice
optionD: a and b are both set to 10 in turn
correctAnswerText: a is set to 5, b is set to a, a is then set to 10, and b is still 5
explanation: The point is that changing one leaves the other alone, which needs a copy followed by a change. The first alternative sets both to the same value without ever copying, so the concept is absent.

prompt: A teacher wants an example showing that an average of whole numbers can lose its fraction. They choose the values 4 and 8. Each option below is a genuine example of something. What is wrong with their choice?
optionA: The values are too small to show the effect
optionB: Two values are too few for an average
optionC: The average of 4 and 8 is exactly 6, so nothing is lost and the point does not appear
optionD: Nothing; the example is fine
correctAnswerText: The average of 4 and 8 is exactly 6, so nothing is lost and the point does not appear
explanation: An example has to make the concept visible, and values that divide exactly hide it completely. Choosing 4 and 7 instead would show the loss immediately, which is the whole difference between a demonstration and an illustration.

prompt: A simplification says "memory is where the computer keeps things it is using". Does it leave a false belief?
optionA: Yes; it implies memory keeps things permanently
optionB: No; it omits detail without implying anything untrue
optionC: Yes; it implies memory is the only place things are kept
optionD: Yes; it implies memory is a physical place
correctAnswerText: No; it omits detail without implying anything untrue
explanation: The statement is incomplete and not misleading: it says nothing about persistence either way. A harmful simplification produces a prediction that turns out wrong.

prompt: A simplification says "saving a file puts it in memory so you can get it back later". A student who believes it does not save before switching off. The statement is short and reads clearly. What is wrong with it?
optionA: It is too short to be useful
optionB: It omits how saving works internally
optionC: Nothing; the student should have known better
optionD: It puts saved files in memory, which produces a false prediction about switching off
correctAnswerText: It puts saved files in memory, which produces a false prediction about switching off
explanation: The simplification does not merely leave something out; it puts a file in the wrong place and the reader acts on that. The test of a simplification is whether the beliefs it creates are true as far as they go.

prompt: A team chose to keep a collection sorted. Which account explains the decision?
optionA: Because the collection is searched far more often than it is added to, and searching sorted data is much cheaper
optionB: Because they decided sorting was the right approach
optionC: Because sorted data is standard practice
optionD: Because sorting is a well-understood operation
correctAnswerText: Because the collection is searched far more often than it is added to, and searching sorted data is much cheaper
explanation: Only one account gives a reason tied to this situation. Convention and familiarity would support any decision equally and so explain none.

prompt: A team chose to store a value in the browser rather than on the server, and justified it by saying "it is simpler". Simplicity would also have justified storing it on the server. What is wrong with the justification?
optionA: It is not a real consideration
optionB: It is too short
optionC: It does not distinguish the option chosen from the one rejected, so it explains nothing
optionD: Nothing; simplicity is a valid reason
correctAnswerText: It does not distinguish the option chosen from the one rejected, so it explains nothing
explanation: Simplicity is a genuine consideration and here it points both ways, so it cannot be why one was chosen. A reason that would equally support the alternative is the sharpest kind of non-explanation.

prompt: A student believes the processor is where files are kept. Which response would change that belief?
optionA: Tell them the processor does not keep files
optionB: Ask where the files are when the machine is switched off, and follow that to storage
optionC: Explain how the processor executes instructions
optionD: Tell them files are kept on storage
correctAnswerText: Ask where the files are when the machine is switched off, and follow that to storage
explanation: A correction that engages the belief lets the student see for themselves why it cannot hold. Simply asserting the opposite leaves them with two claims and no way to choose.

prompt: A student believes a loop always runs its body at least once. A colleague replies, correctly, that a test-first loop checks before running. The reply is accurate and the student is unconvinced. What is missing?
optionA: A more precise definition of a loop
optionB: An example of a loop that never ends
optionC: Nothing; the reply is correct
optionD: An account of why the belief seemed right — most loops they have written did run at least once
correctAnswerText: An account of why the belief seemed right — most loops they have written did run at least once
explanation: A belief formed from experience is not dislodged by a contrary statement, however accurate. Showing why the experience was consistent with it, and where it stops being so, is what changes it.

prompt: A student believes a program works out what they meant when the input is unexpected. Which correction would change the belief most durably?
optionA: Show a case where the unexpected input produces plainly wrong behaviour that nobody wrote
optionB: Tell them programs only do what they are told
optionC: Explain how a processor executes instructions
optionD: Give them a definition of a program
correctAnswerText: Show a case where the unexpected input produces plainly wrong behaviour that nobody wrote
explanation: A belief about behaviour is best corrected by behaviour, because the student sees the prediction fail. A general statement is easy to accept and easy to keep acting against.

prompt: Why is contradicting a misconception often less effective than explaining why it seemed reasonable?
optionA: Because contradiction is impolite
optionB: Because people never change their minds
optionC: The belief was formed from evidence, and evidence that is not accounted for keeps supporting it
optionD: Because a misconception is usually partly true
correctAnswerText: The belief was formed from evidence, and evidence that is not accounted for keeps supporting it
explanation: Somebody holding a wrong belief usually has reasons, and a bare contradiction leaves those reasons standing. Accounting for them is what makes the correction stick rather than being accepted and then forgotten.

prompt: A misconception is corrected and the student agrees, then makes the same mistake a week later. What does that suggest?
optionA: The student was not paying attention
optionB: The correction was accepted without replacing the model that produced the mistake
optionC: The correction was wrong
optionD: Misconceptions cannot be corrected
correctAnswerText: The correction was accepted without replacing the model that produced the mistake
explanation: Agreeing with a statement and holding a working model are different things, and only the second governs what somebody does under pressure. That the mistake recurs is evidence about the correction rather than about the student.

prompt: An explanation reads: "The page is stale because of caching." The named fault is that it does not say what caching did here. The sentence is accurate and clearly written. Which change fixes that fault?
optionA: "The page is stale because of caching, which is a common problem."
optionB: "The page is stale. Caching stores copies of files to improve performance."
optionC: "The page appears to be stale because of caching behaviour."
optionD: "The page is stale because your browser reused a stored copy instead of fetching the new file."
correctAnswerText: "The page is stale because your browser reused a stored copy instead of fetching the new file."
explanation: Only one option says what happened in this case. The others add sympathy, general background, or hedging — each an improvement of some kind that leaves the named fault untouched.

prompt: An explanation reads: "Saving writes the file to memory." The named fault is that it is inaccurate. Which change fixes it without introducing a new fault?
optionA: "Saving writes the file to storage, which keeps it after the machine is switched off."
optionB: "Saving writes the file to memory, which keeps it after the machine is switched off."
optionC: "Saving writes the file to storage, and storage is a kind of memory."
optionD: "Saving preserves the file."
correctAnswerText: "Saving writes the file to storage, which keeps it after the machine is switched off."
explanation: The first correction replaces the wrong place with the right one and says why it matters. The second keeps the error, the third reintroduces the confusion by another route, and the fourth is true and says nothing.

prompt: An explanation reads: "The request failed because the server returned an error." The named fault is circularity. Which change fixes it?
optionA: "The request failed because the server responded with a failure status."
optionB: "The request failed. Servers return errors when something goes wrong."
optionC: "The request failed because it was missing the identification the server requires."
optionD: "The request was unsuccessful because the server did not succeed."
correctAnswerText: "The request failed because it was missing the identification the server requires."
explanation: Only one option supplies something other than the failure itself. The other three restate it in fresh words, which is what circularity survives on.

prompt: An explanation has two faults: it is inaccurate about one step, and it assumes a term the reader does not know. Only one can be repaired before it is sent. Which should it be?
optionA: The unknown term, because the reader cannot get past it
optionB: The inaccuracy, because a reader who follows it will believe something false, while an unknown term leaves them asking
optionC: Either; both are defects of the same kind
optionD: Neither; an explanation with two faults should not be sent
correctAnswerText: The inaccuracy, because a reader who follows it will believe something false, while an unknown term leaves them asking
explanation: A term the reader cannot follow stops them and prompts a question; an inaccuracy they can follow is absorbed. Ranking defects by what the reader ends up believing is what makes a single repair a decision.

prompt: A repair removes a named fault and makes the explanation noticeably longer. When is that a poor trade?
optionA: Always; explanations should be as short as possible
optionB: Never; correctness outweighs length
optionC: When the reader is an expert
optionD: When the added length pushes the part that answers the question past where the reader stops reading
correctAnswerText: When the added length pushes the part that answers the question past where the reader stops reading
explanation: Length matters through whether the explanation is read to the point that matters. A longer version that leads with the answer costs almost nothing, and one that buries it costs everything.

prompt: An explanation written for developers reads: "The endpoint is idempotent, so retries are safe." It must be rewritten for a support agent who knows the product and not the vocabulary. The meaning must be preserved. Which version works?
optionA: "Sending the same request again does not do the action twice, so it is safe to retry."
optionB: "The endpoint is idempotent, so retries are safe. Please retry."
optionC: "Retries are safe."
optionD: "The endpoint has a property that makes retrying acceptable."
correctAnswerText: "Sending the same request again does not do the action twice, so it is safe to retry."
explanation: Only one option removes the term and keeps what it meant. Shortening keeps the assumed knowledge or drops the substance, and naming the property without saying what it is leaves the reader exactly where they started.

prompt: An explanation for a first-year is being rewritten for a complete beginner. What is the main risk?
optionA: Making it too long
optionB: Using an analogy
optionC: Removing the vocabulary and the substance together, leaving something true and empty
optionD: Explaining something the reader already knows
correctAnswerText: Removing the vocabulary and the substance together, leaving something true and empty
explanation: Simplifying by deletion is the easy failure: what remains is accurate and carries no meaning. An analogy is a tool rather than a risk, provided its limits are known.

prompt: An explanation is rewritten for a non-technical reader by replacing every technical term with an analogy. What is the risk?
optionA: There is no risk; analogies always help
optionB: The analogies carry conclusions the technical terms did not, so the reader may believe things that are false
optionC: The explanation becomes longer
optionD: The reader will not understand the analogies
correctAnswerText: The analogies carry conclusions the technical terms did not, so the reader may believe things that are false
explanation: Every analogy supports conclusions of its own, and a chain of them supports a great many. Replacing terms wholesale trades one kind of inaccessibility for a different kind of inaccuracy.

prompt: One explanation must serve both a first-year student and an experienced developer. What is the best approach?
optionA: Write at the level of the less experienced reader throughout
optionB: Write at the level of the more experienced reader throughout
optionC: Write two separate explanations and hope each reader finds theirs
optionD: Answer the question plainly first, then add the detail the experienced reader needs below it
correctAnswerText: Answer the question plainly first, then add the detail the experienced reader needs below it
explanation: Ordering by depth lets each reader stop where their need is met, which is what a single document can do that two cannot. Pitching throughout at either level fails one of the two readers by design.
